title: Latency, Throughput, Jitter and Packet Loss
objectives: Define and distinguish latency, throughput, jitter and packet loss, and state which one a given symptom is
Compute serialization delay for a frame at a given line rate and the bandwidth-delay product of a path
Decompose an end-to-end latency budget into additive components and optimize the largest term first
Explain why percentile latencies (p99) - not means - are the operational target, and how loss rates convert into gap rates
motivation: Two firms colocated in the same datacenter run identical strategies; one fills 40 µs after the tick, the other 400 µs - and loses the queue position that decides the trade. The gap is not bandwidth (both have 10 Gb/s) but latency arithmetic: serialization, hops, jitter tails and the occasional lost packet. This lesson gives you the four metrics, the formulas behind them, and the discipline of decomposing a budget instead of guessing.

blocks.text: Four numbers that describe a network

blocks.md: **Latency** is the time one message takes from A to B (one-way) or A→B→A (round trip). **Throughput** is the data rate sustained over time - bits per second - and is a *rate*, not a time; a 10 Gb/s link is not 'fast at delivering one packet', it is wide at delivering many. **Jitter** is the variation of latency between packets: the p99 that ruins assumptions made on the mean. **Loss** is the fraction of datagrams the network drops. The four interact: near-capacity queues create jitter and loss; TCP turns loss into retransmission latency; and a strategy tuned for the mean latency gets destroyed by the tail. Measuring one-way latency also requires synchronized clocks (PTP in serious setups), which is why round-trip time (RTT) - measurable with timestamps at one machine - is the everyday metric and one-way figures are derived carefully.

blocks.tex: T_{\text{end-to-end}} = T_{\text{NIC}} + T_{\text{kernel}} + T_{\text{strategy}} + T_{\text{NIC,out}} + T_{\text{wire}}
blocks.caption: A tick-to-trade budget decomposes additively - optimize the largest term first, because halving a small term changes nothing.

blocks.text: Serialization delay and the bandwidth-delay product

blocks.md: The first unavoidable latency term is **serialization delay**: even an unloaded link needs time to clock a frame's bits onto the wire. It is frame size divided by line rate - so bigger frames cost more *time* on the same link, while higher line rates shrink the time. The mirror-image quantity is the **bandwidth-delay product (BDP)**: how many bits a link holds in flight when it is kept full. It equals bandwidth × RTT and tells you how much data (or how big a buffer) is needed to saturate a path - the reason fat, long links feel 'slow' for small, stop-and-wait request/response patterns no matter how wide they are.

blocks.title: Worked example: 10 Gb/s arithmetic
items: A 1500-byte frame on a 10 Gb/s link: $1500 \times 8 / 10^{10} = 12{,}000$ ns $= 1.2$ µs of serialization - the wire itself needs that long even with zero queueing.
Bandwidth-delay product with a 100 µs RTT: $10^{10} \times 100 \times 10^{-6} = 10^6$ bits $= 125{,}000$ bytes in flight to keep the path busy.
Loss arithmetic: at 200,000 messages/s, a 0.01% loss rate is $200{,}000 \times 0.0001 = 20$ gaps per second - each demanding a retransmission (TCP, costing ≥ 1 RTT) or a feed-level gap recovery.
A hypothetical tick-to-trade budget of 5 µs splits, say, 1 µs NIC-in, 0.5 µs kernel, 2 µs strategy, 1 µs NIC-out, 0.5 µs wire - and the 2 µs strategy term is the only one worth optimizing first.

blocks.md: Where does jitter come from? **Queueing**. A switch buffers bursts; buffer occupancy depends on what other traffic did microseconds earlier, so per-packet delay wanders - especially as utilization approaches capacity, where queues grow steeply and nonlinearly. At 90% utilization a link's queue behaves very differently from 50%. The operational consequence: report and optimize **percentiles**, not means. If 1,000 messages have a mean latency of 5 µs but p99 is 40 µs, one message in a hundred arrives eight times late - and a queue-position race is lost on the tail, not the average. Tail latency is why low-latency systems measure p99/p999 and why jitter (tail spread) often matters more than mean latency itself.

blocks.caption: Per-packet delay under bursts wanders like a random walk: the mean of this path says little about the spikes that decide queue races. Monitor p99, not the mean.

blocks.md: On TCP, a lost segment costs at least an RTT (fast retransmit) and can cost orders of magnitude more on timeouts; on a UDP feed, loss becomes an application gap detected by sequence number and repaired via a retransmission channel - still a full RTT plus server work. Loss also correlates with the queueing that causes jitter, so the tail of the latency distribution and the loss rate rise *together* near saturation. This is the engineering case for headroom: trading networks run well below capacity, because the last 10% of throughput costs disproportionate tail latency and loss.

blocks.title: Tick-to-trade as a budget review
blocks.md: Production desks treat tick-to-trade as a table of additive terms owned by different teams (NIC, kernel bypass, strategy code, wire). The rule is Amdahl-flavoured: a 2x improvement on a 0.5 µs term buys 0.25 µs; the same effort on the 2 µs strategy term buys 1 µs. Measure each term with hardware timestamps, rank by size, and attack in order - never optimize the term that is merely the most interesting.

guidedExercise.prompt: A 512-byte market-data message leaves a 10 Gb/s NIC, crosses one unloaded switch, and travels 300 ns of combined propagation and switching delay (store-and-forward at the switch is already included). (a) Compute the serialization delay in nanoseconds. (b) Compute the total one-way latency in nanoseconds. (c) If the strategy code adds 1.5 µs and outbound NIC processing 0.4 µs, what is the tick-to-decision time in µs?
hints: Additive budgets: sum the terms, then convert units once at the end.
guidedExercise.solution: (a) $512 \times 8 = 4096$ bits; $4096 / 10^{10} = 409.6$ ns $\approx 0.41$ µs. (b) $409.6 + 300 = 709.6$ ns $\approx 0.71$ µs. (c) $0.71 + 1.5 + 0.4 = 2.61$ µs - and the strategy term dominates the budget, so that is where optimization pays.

independentExercise.prompt: A disaster-recovery link runs at 40 Gb/s with an 80 µs RTT. (a) Compute the bandwidth-delay product in kilobytes. (b) An application sends a request, waits for the full response, then sends the next (stop-and-wait). Explain, using the BDP, why the link cannot approach 40 Gb/s this way. (c) The feed across the same path delivers 400,000 messages/s; a 0.005% loss rate causes how many gaps per second? (d) If each TCP recovery costs 2 RTTs, what total time per second is spent in recovery (in ms)?
hints: Stop-and-wait sends one BDP-sized window's worth of nothing between packets.
Loss rate × message rate = gap rate.
independentExercise.solution: (a) $40 \times 10^9 \times 80 \times 10^{-6} = 3.2 \times 10^6$ bits $= 400{,}000$ bytes $\approx 390$ KB (in flight to keep the pipe full). (b) Stop-and-wait keeps at most one small message in flight against a 3.2 Mb pipe, so throughput is bounded by RTT × message count, not bandwidth - utilization is tiny no matter the line rate. (c) $400{,}000 \times 0.00005 = 20$ gaps/s. (d) $20 \times 2 \times 80$ µs $= 3200$ µs $= 3.2$ ms per second spent recovering - small on average, but each gap delays one decision by 160 µs.

commonMistakes: Confusing throughput with latency - a wider link does not make one small packet arrive sooner; it makes many packets per second possible.
Optimizing the mean instead of the tail - queue-position races are decided by p99/p999, and means hide exactly the events that lose money.
Forgetting serialization delay on large frames and then blaming 'the switch' for the missing microseconds.
Treating a 0.01% loss rate as negligible at high message rates - 200,000 msgs/s × 0.01% is 20 gaps every second, each costing an RTT to repair.
realWorldApplication: CDN providers, HFT firms and cloud operators all publish percentile-based SLAs (p50/p99/p999) because averages are marketing; queueing theory's steep delay curve near capacity is why every network is provisioned with headroom.
quantFinanceApplication: Tick-to-trade budgets are decomposed and reviewed term by term (NIC, kernel, strategy, wire); a firm at 40 µs p50 but 400 µs p99 loses precisely the races that decide whether a hedge lands before the price moves.
summary: Latency is time per message, throughput is bits per second, jitter is latency variation, loss is dropped datagrams; they interact through queues.
Serialization delay = frame bits / line rate (1500 B at 10 Gb/s = 1.2 µs); BDP = bandwidth × RTT (10 Gb/s × 100 µs = 125 KB in flight).
End-to-end budgets are additive: optimize the largest term first, and report p99 not the mean because queues make delay wander.
Loss converts to gap rate = loss rate × message rate (0.01% of 200k msgs/s = 20 gaps/s), each costing ~an RTT to repair - headroom on links is cheaper than tail latency.

quiz.prompt: What is the serialization delay of a 1500-byte frame on a 10 Gb/s link, in microseconds?
quiz.explanation: $1500 \times 8 / 10^{10} = 12{,}000$ ns $= 1.2$ µs - bits onto the wire, even with no queueing.

quiz.prompt: What is the bandwidth-delay product of a 10 Gb/s link with a 100 µs RTT, in kilobytes?
quiz.explanation: $10^{10} \times 100 \times 10^{-6} = 10^6$ bits $= 125{,}000$ bytes $= 125$ KB must be in flight to keep the path busy.

options: The average one-way delay across a path
The variation of latency from packet to packet
The maximum sustainable bits per second
The fraction of datagrams the network discards
quiz.explanation: Jitter is latency *variation* - usually caused by queueing behind bursts. The mean delay, throughput and loss rate are the other three metrics.

quiz.prompt: A feed delivers 200,000 messages/s and the network drops 0.01% of datagrams. How many gaps per second does the consumer detect?
quiz.explanation: $200{,}000 \times 0.0001 = 20$ gaps/s - 'small' percentages are large at feed rates.

quiz.prompt: Which statements about latency budgets and monitoring are true?
options: Percentiles (p99) are a better operational target than the mean for trading systems
Throughput and latency are independent - you can always raise one without touching the other
Queueing delay rises sharply and nonlinearly as link utilization approaches 100%
Packet loss only matters to TCP connections, never to UDP feeds
quiz.explanation: Tails decide races and delay grows steeply near capacity - both true. The other two are wrong: at high utilization they are coupled, and UDP feed consumers detect loss as sequence gaps that cost recovery time.

quiz.prompt: What is the industry term for the end-to-end time from observing a market data update to the corresponding order leaving the firm's network?
quiz.modelAnswer: Tick-to-trade time - the additive budget from market data arrival to outbound order, decomposed across NIC, kernel, strategy and wire.
quiz.explanation: Tick-to-trade is the standard headline metric, always quoted at percentiles and reviewed as an additive budget.

flashcards.back: Latency = time for one message (ns-µs); throughput = sustained bits/s. Wider links help the second, not the first - and near capacity, throughput gains cost tail latency.
$T = \text{bits} / \text{line rate}$; 1500 B at 10 Gb/s = 1.2 µs, 64 B = 51.2 ns.
Packet-to-packet variation in latency, driven by queueing behind bursts; it widens the tail, so p99 - not the mean - is the operational number.
gaps/s = message rate × loss fraction; 200,000 msgs/s at 0.01% = 20 gaps/s, each repaired at ~1+ RTT.
